claim: Spermidine and other polyamines alleviate oxidative stress.
source: Spermidine and other polyamines alleviate oxidative stress, yet excess spermidine seems toxic to Escherichia coli unless it is neutralized by SpeG, an enzyme for the spermidine N-acetyl transferase function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about polyamines.

claim: Excess spermidine is toxic to Escherichia coli unless it is neutralized by SpeG.
source: Spermidine and other polyamines alleviate oxidative stress, yet excess spermidine seems toxic to Escherichia coli unless it is neutralized by SpeG, an enzyme for the spermidine N-acetyl transferase function.
evidence: This is a central premise of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: SpeG is an enzyme with spermidine N-acetyl transferase function.
source: Spermidine and other polyamines alleviate oxidative stress, yet excess spermidine seems toxic to Escherichia coli unless it is neutralized by SpeG, an enzyme for the spermidine N-acetyl transferase function.
evidence: This is stated as a known function of SpeG in the abstract.

claim: Wild-type E. coli can tolerate applied exogenous spermidine stress.
source: Thus, wild-type E. coli can tolerate applied exogenous spermidine stress, but ΔspeG strain of E. coli fails to do that.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key observation.

claim: ΔspeG strain of E. coli fails to tolerate applied exogenous spermidine stress.
source: Thus, wild-type E. coli can tolerate applied exogenous spermidine stress, but ΔspeG strain of E. coli fails to do that.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key observation.

claim: Spermidine mitigates oxidative stress by lowering overall ROS levels.
source: Here, using different reactive oxygen species (ROS) probes and performing electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, we provide evidence that although spermidine mitigates oxidative stress by lowering overall ROS levels, excess of it simultaneously triggers the production of superoxide radicals, thereby causing toxicity in the ΔspeG strain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using ROS probes and EPR spectroscopy as stated in the abstract.

claim: Excess spermidine simultaneously triggers the production of superoxide radicals.
source: Here, using different reactive oxygen species (ROS) probes and performing electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, we provide evidence that although spermidine mitigates oxidative stress by lowering overall ROS levels, excess of it simultaneously triggers the production of superoxide radicals, thereby causing toxicity in the ΔspeG strain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using ROS probes and EPR spectroscopy as stated in the abstract.

claim: Excess spermidine causes toxicity in the ΔspeG strain through superoxide radical production.
source: Here, using different reactive oxygen species (ROS) probes and performing electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, we provide evidence that although spermidine mitigates oxidative stress by lowering overall ROS levels, excess of it simultaneously triggers the production of superoxide radicals, thereby causing toxicity in the ΔspeG strain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Spermidine-induced superoxide anions affect redox balance.
source: Furthermore, performing microarray experiment and other biochemical assays, we show that the spermidine-induced superoxide anions affected redox balance and iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by microarray and biochemical assay data as stated in the abstract.

claim: Spermidine-induced superoxide anions affect iron homeostasis.
source: Furthermore, performing microarray experiment and other biochemical assays, we show that the spermidine-induced superoxide anions affected redox balance and iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by microarray and biochemical assay data as stated in the abstract.

claim: RNA-bound spermidine inhibits iron oxidation.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that while RNA-bound spermidine inhibits iron oxidation, free spermidine interacts and oxidizes the iron to evoke superoxide radicals directly.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data as stated in the abstract.

claim: Free spermidine interacts and oxidizes iron to evoke superoxide radicals directly.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that while RNA-bound spermidine inhibits iron oxidation, free spermidine interacts and oxidizes the iron to evoke superoxide radicals directly.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data as stated in the abstract.

claim: Spermidine-induced superoxide generation is one of the major causes of spermidine toxicity in E. coli.
source: Therefore, we propose that the spermidine-induced superoxide generation is one of the major causes of spermidine toxicity in E. coli.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Polyamines tweak a diverse array of biological processes including nucleic acid and protein metabolism, ion channel functions, cell growth and differentiation, mitochondrial function, autophagy and aging, protection from oxidative damage, and actin polymerization.
source: They tweak a diverse array of biological processes, for example, nucleic acid and protein metabolism, ion channel functions, cell growth and differentiation, mitochondrial function, autophagy and aging, protection from oxidative damage, actin polymerization, and perhaps many more (Casero et al., 2018; Gawlitta et al., 1981; Madeo et al., 2018; Michael, 2018; Miller-Fleming et al., 2015; Oriol-Audit, 1978; Pegg, 2016; Pohjanpelto et al., 1981; Tabor and Tabor, 1984; Wallace et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The cationic amine groups of polyamines can avidly bind to negatively charged molecules such as RNA, DNA, and phospholipids.
source: The cationic amine groups of polyamines can avidly bind to the negatively charged molecules, such as RNA, DNA, phospholipids, etc. (Igarashi and Kashiwagi, 2000; Miyamoto et al., 1993; Schuber, 1989; Tabor and Tabor, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyamines protect DNA from reactive oxygen species such as singlet oxygen, hydroxyl radical, or hydrogen peroxide.
source: Polyamines have been demonstrated to protect DNA from reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as singlet oxygen, hydroxyl radical (•OH), or hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) (Balasundaram et al., 1993; Ha et al., 1998a; Ha et al., 1998b; Jung and Kim, 2003; Khan et al., 1992a; Khan et al., 1992b; LØVaas, 1996; Pegg, 2018; Murray Stewart et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Knocking out polyamine biosynthesis enzymes from E. coli and yeast confers toxicity to oxygen, superoxide anion radical, and H2O2.
source: Indeed, knocking out polyamine biosynthesis enzymes from Escherichia coli and yeast confers toxicity to oxygen, superoxide anion radical (O2-), and H2O2 (Balasundaram et al., 1993; Chattopadhyay et al., 2003; Eisenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most prokaryotes including E. coli synthesize cadaverine, putrescine, and spermidine.
source: Most prokaryotes including E. coli synthesize cadaverine, putrescine, and spermidine, while higher eukaryotes additionally synthesize spermine.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about polyamine biosynthesis.

claim: Higher eukaryotes additionally synthesize spermine.
source: Most prokaryotes including E. coli synthesize cadaverine, putrescine, and spermidine, while higher eukaryotes additionally synthesize spermine.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about polyamine biosynthesis.

claim: E. coli acquires spermidine and putrescine from the surrounding medium.
source: E. coli also acquires spermidine and putrescine from the surrounding medium (Igarashi and Kashiwagi, 2000; Miller-Fleming et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyamine in excess is toxic to organisms unless polyamine homeostasis is operated at the levels of export, synthesis, inactivation, and degradation.
source: However, polyamine in excess is toxic to the organisms unless polyamine homeostasis in the cell is operated at the levels of export, synthesis, inactivation, and degradation (Miller-Fleming et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spermine/spermidine N-acetyl transferase (SSAT or SpeG) constitutes the most potent polyamine homeostasis component of cells.
source: Notably, spermine/spermidine N-acetyl transferase (SSAT or SpeG), which inactivates spermidine and spermine, constitutes the most potent polyamine homeostasis component of the cells (Miller-Fleming et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spermidine or spermine in excess is toxic to organisms and viruses.
source: It has also been known for long that spermidine (or spermine) in excess is toxic to the organisms and viruses (Pegg, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Excess polyamines may affect protein synthesis by binding to acidic sites in macromolecules and displacing magnesium from these sites.
source: It has been proposed that the excess polyamines may affect protein synthesis by binding to acidic sites in macromolecules, such as nucleic acids, proteins, and membrane, and by displacing magnesium from these sites (Limsuwun and Jones, 2000; Pegg, 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A precise molecular detail of spermidine toxicity is not yet understood.
source: However, a precise molecular detail of spermidine toxicity is not yet understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: WT cells showed a modest reduction in growth up to 6.4 mM of spermidine concentration.
source: WT cells showed a modest reduction in growth up to 6.4 mM of spermidine concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ΔspeG strain exhibited a striking decrease in growth when supplemental spermidine level was >3.2 mM.
source: On the contrary, ΔspeG strain exhibited a striking decrease in growth when supplemental spermidine level was >3.2 mM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Supplementation of 3.2 mM exogenous spermidine in the growth medium increased the intracellular spermidine levels in the ΔspeG strain.
source: Supplementation of 3.2 mM exogenous spermidine in the growth medium increased the intracellular spermidine levels in the ΔspeG strain, while no significant increase was observed in the WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant increase in intracellular spermidine was observed in WT cells upon supplementation of 3.2 mM exogenous spermidine.
source: Supplementation of 3.2 mM exogenous spermidine in the growth medium increased the intracellular spermidine levels in the ΔspeG strain, while no significant increase was observed in the WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SpeG function converts excess spermidine to N1- and N8-acetyl-spermidines maintaining the level of spermidine in WT cells.
source: The SpeG function apparently converted the excess spermidine to N1- and N8-acetyl-spermidines maintaining the level of spermidine in the WT cells (Miller-Fleming et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by a citation.

claim: The spermidine synthase-defective (ΔspeE) strain of E. coli acquired spermidine at a low level from the LB medium.
source: The spermidine synthase-defective (ΔspeE) strain of E. coli also acquired spermidine at a low level from the LB medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Polyamine spermidine is an anti-ROS agent.
source: It is well documented that polyamine spermidine is an anti-ROS agent (Balasundaram et al., 1993; Chattopadhyay et al., 2003; Chattopadhyay et al., 2006; Ha et al., 1998a; Khan et al., 1992a; Khan et al., 1992b; Pegg, 2018; Murray Stewart et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: All in vivo studies in the past have been conducted under polyamine deficient conditions to show ROS production.
source: However, all the in vivo studies in the past have been conducted under polyamine deficient conditions to show ROS production, thereby implicating the anti-ROS function of polyamines.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous studies.

claim: The relative mean fluorescence intensity of H2DCFDA was increased about 1.5-fold in the spermidine synthase-defective (ΔspeE) strain.
source: The relative mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of H2DCFDA was increased about 1.5-fold in the spermidine synthase-defective (ΔspeE) strain, while no change in MFI was observed in the ΔspeG strain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No change in H2DCFDA MFI was observed in the ΔspeG strain.
source: The relative mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of H2DCFDA was increased about 1.5-fold in the spermidine synthase-defective (ΔspeE) strain, while no change in MFI was observed in the ΔspeG strain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Spermidine treatment significantly decreased the H2DCFDA fluorescence in WT, ΔspeG, and ΔspeE strains.
source: However, spermidine treatment significantly decreased the H2DCFDA fluorescence in WT, ΔspeG, and ΔspeE strains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Despite no apparent increase in the spermidine level in WT cells under spermidine stress, a significant decrease in the H2DCFDA fluorescence was observed.
source: Interestingly, despite no apparent increase in the spermidine level in WT cells under spermidine stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a significant decrease in the H2DCFDA fluorescence was observed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The acetylated products of spermidine might have some role in the declined ROS levels causing decreased H2DCFDA fluorescence in spermidine-fed WT cells.
source: It is possible that the acetylated products of spermidine might have some role in the declined ROS levels causing decreased H2DCFDA fluorescence in spermidine-fed WT cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data.

claim: The relative MFI of DHE probe was increased significantly (1.5-fold) in ΔspeE strain.
source: Similarly, the relative MFI of DHE probe was increased significantly (1.5-fold) in ΔspeE strain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The relative MFI of DHE probe was increased significantly (2-fold) in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG as compared to WT strain of E. coli.
source: Surprisingly, the relative MFI of DHE probe was increased significantly (2-fold) in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG as compared to WT strain of E. coli (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tyron (Tr), an O2- quencher, decreased the MFI of DHE in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain.
source: Tyron (Tr), an O2- quencher, decreased the MFI of DHE in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ΔspeE and spermidine-fed ΔspeG strains release substantially low levels of H2O2 compared to the untreated counterpart and WT cells.
source: In another assay, we determined that the ΔspeE and spermidine-fed ΔspeG strains release substantially low levels of H2O2 compared to the untreated counterpart and WT cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by H2O2 measurement data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A far wider zone of inhibition (ZOI) of growth for ΔspeG strain was observed compared to WT under aerobic condition.
source: A far wider zone of inhibition (ZOI) of growth for ΔspeG strain was observed compared to WT under aerobic condition (Figure 1D), while a narrow ZOI was observed under anaerobic conditions for both strains (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A narrow ZOI was observed under anaerobic conditions for both WT and ΔspeG strains.
source: A far wider zone of inhibition (ZOI) of growth for ΔspeG strain was observed compared to WT under aerobic condition (Figure 1D), while a narrow ZOI was observed under anaerobic conditions for both strains (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: O2- production in aerobic condition could be a cause of the observed spermidine toxicity.
source: This data further indicates that O2- production in aerobic condition could be a cause of the observed spermidine toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ZOI data under aerobic vs anaerobic conditions.

claim: The ΔspeGΔsodA and ΔspeGΔsodAΔsodB mutants containing empty vector exhibited higher growth defects than ΔspeG strain on LB-agar plate supplemented with spermidine.
source: The ΔspeGΔsodA and ΔspeGΔsodAΔsodB mutants containing empty vector exhibited higher growth defects than ΔspeG strain on LB-agar plate supplemented with spermidine (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The cell viability of the double mutants was similar to the ΔspeG strain, while the triple mutant exhibited an accelerated loss of cell viability, in the presence of spermidine.
source: However, the cell viability of the double mutants was similar to the ΔspeG strain, while the triple mutant exhibited an accelerated loss of cell viability, in the presence of spermidine (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The multicopy induction of SodA from pSodA plasmid suppressed the growth defect in the ΔspeG and ΔspeGΔsodA strains.
source: The multicopy induction of SodA from pSodA plasmid suppressed the growth defect in the ΔspeG and ΔspeGΔsodA strains (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The overexpression of SodA improved the viability of ΔspeGΔsodA strain.
source: The overexpression of SodA also improved the viability of ΔspeGΔsodA strain (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The single mutants show growth and viability similar to the WT strain in the presence or absence of spermidine.
source: Note that, unlike ΔspeG strain, the single mutants show growth and viability similar to the WT strain in the presence or absence of spermidine (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of SOD enzymes aggravates O2- toxicity in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain.
source: This data suggests that the absence of SOD enzymes aggravates O2- toxicity in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the growth and viability data of SOD mutants.

claim: Spermidine transport is a proton motif force (PMF)-dependent process.
source: Spermidine transport is a proton motif force (PMF)-dependent process (Kashiwagi et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The observed narrower ZOI in the presence of spermidine under anaerobic condition could be due to the low PMF under anaerobic condition.
source: Therefore, the observed narrower ZOI in the presence of spermidine under anaerobic condition (Figure 1D) could also be due to the low PMF under anaerobic condition.
evidence: This is a speculation about an alternative explanation for the observed data.

claim: CMH reacts at a much faster rate with O2- anion, producing highly stable and EPR-sensitive nitroxide radicals.
source: Compared to spin-trap agents, lower level of CMH reacts at a much faster rate with O2- anion, producing highly stable and EPR-sensitive nitroxide radicals (Dikalov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Peroxynitrite and •OH radicals can also oxidize CMH.
source: However, peroxynitrite and •OH radicals can also oxidize CMH (Dikalov et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A high level of EPR signals were detected with more signal in the unfed sample than the spermidine-fed one in the first set of EPR experiments.
source: In the first set, a high level of EPR signals were detected with more signal in the unfed sample than the spermidine-fed one (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by EPR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The overall ROS production is higher in the absence of exogenous spermidine.
source: This data indicates that the overall ROS production is higher in the absence of exogenous spermidine, which is consistent with the notion that the spermidine is an anti-ROS agent (Balasundaram et al., 1993; Chattopadhyay et al., 2003; Chattopadhyay et al., 2006; Ha et al., 1998b; Khan et al., 1992a; Khan et al., 1992b; Pegg, 2018; Murray Stewart et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference from the EPR data and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: EPR signal was higher in the spermidine-fed cells than unfed one in the second set of EPR experiments.
source: In contrast, EPR signal was higher in the spermidine-fed cells than unfed one in the second set (Figure 2D and E), suggesting that the signals apparently represent CMH oxidation by O2- anions.
evidence: This is supported by EPR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The EPR signals in the second set apparently represent CMH oxidation by O2- anions.
source: In contrast, EPR signal was higher in the spermidine-fed cells than unfed one in the second set (Figure 2D and E), suggesting that the signals apparently represent CMH oxidation by O2- anions.
evidence: This is an inference from the EPR data in the presence of scavengers.

claim: The decrease in EPR signals under the multicopy expression of SodA suggests that the signals in the second set were indeed generated from O2--mediated oxidation of CMH.
source: Finally, the decrease in EPR signals under the multicopy expression of SodA (Figure 2F and G) suggests that the signals in the second set were indeed generated from O2--mediated oxidation of CMH.
evidence: This is an inference from the EPR data with SodA overexpression.

claim: Tr, NAC, and ascorbate, but not SP and TU, rescued the spermidine-mediated growth inhibition phenotype.
source: We show that Tr, NAC, and ascorbate, but not SP and TU, rescued the spermidine-mediated growth inhibition phenotype (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The O2- stress-derived redox imbalance could be the route of spermidine toxicity.
source: This observation further suggests that the O2- stress-derived redox imbalance could be the route of spermidine toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue experiments with antioxidants.

claim: Both the growth and viability of ΔspeGΔzwf double mutant were significantly affected compared to the ΔspeG strain under spermidine stress.
source: We show that both the growth and viability of ΔspeGΔzwf double mutant were significantly affected compared to the ΔspeG strain under spermidine stress (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by growth and viability data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Complementing ΔspeGΔzwf with a plasmid, pBAD-zwf, rescues the growth defect and mortality under spermidine stress.
source: Complementing ΔspeGΔzwf with a plasmid, pBAD-zwf, rescues the growth defect and mortality under spermidine stress (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The relative levels of total and reduced species of NADP and GST were decreased significantly in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain.
source: The relative levels of total and reduced species of NADP and GST were decreased significantly in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The levels of total (NADt), oxidized (NAD+), and reduced (NADH) did not alter significantly.
source: However, the levels of total (NADt), oxidized (NAD+), and reduced (NADH) did not alter significantly (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The NAD+ to NADH ratio was significantly increased in the ΔspeG strain compared to WT cells.
source: Nevertheless, the NAD + to NADH ratio was significantly increased in the ΔspeG strain compared to WT cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: No significant increase of the NAD+/NADH ratios was observed by adding spermidine in the growth medium of WT and ΔspeG strain.
source: No significant increase of the ratios was observed by adding spermidine in the growth medium of WT and ΔspeG strain (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The level of ATP was declined in ΔspeG strain compared to the unfed WT.
source: In consistence with the increased ratio of NAD + to NADH, the level of ATP was declined in ΔspeG strain compared to the unfed WT (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by ATP assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ATP level was further decreased in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain.
source: ATP level was further decreased in the spermidine-fed ΔspeG strain (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by ATP assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Genes that were >2-fold downregulated under spermidine stress are involved in flagellar biogenesis, acid resistance, hydrogenase function, nitrogen metabolism, electron transport, aromatic and basic amino acid metabolism.
source: The genes that were >2-fold downregulated are involved in flagellar biogenesis, acid resistance, hydrogenase function, nitrogen metabolism, electron transport, aromatic and basic amino acid metabolism, etc. (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Transcription of the genes encoding chaperones, heat shock, and other stress factors (groL, groS, dnaK, hdeAB, ibpAB, uspAB, etc.) was downregulated under spermidine stress.
source: Interestingly, transcription of the genes encoding chaperones, heat shock, and other stress factors (groL, groS, dnaK, hdeAB, ibpAB, uspAB, etc.) was also downregulated under spermidine stress (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Among the highly upregulated category, the genes that encode for the ribosome, RNA polymerase, transcription factors, DNA polymerase, and enzymes for the fatty acid biosynthesis and iron-sulfur cluster (isc) biogenesis were prominent.
source: On the other hand, among the highly upregulated category, the genes that encode for the ribosome, RNA polymerase, transcription factors, DNA polymerase, and enzymes for the fatty acid biosynthesis and iron-sulfur cluster (isc) biogenesis were prominent (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Excess spermidine could interfere with broad cellular processes, such as protein folding and proteostasis, DNA, RNA and lipid metabolisms, and iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis.
source: These observations indicate that apart from inducing superoxide production (Figures 1 and 2), the excess spermidine could interfere with broad cellular processes, such as protein folding and proteostasis, DNA, RNA and lipid metabolisms, and iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference from the microarray data.

claim: Many operons regulated by Fis and IHF were activated or repressed in the microarray indicating that spermidine could activate Fis and IHF regulon.
source: Many operons regulated by Fis and IHF were activated or repressed in our microarray indicating that spermidine could activate Fis and IHF regulon (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the microarray data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The differential expression of the Fis-regulated operons was significantly enriched (p-value 0.0023).
source: Performing Fisher's exact test, we show that the differential expression of the Fis-regulated operons was significantly enriched (p-value 0.0023).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the microarray data.

claim: ΔspeGΔfis, but not ΔspeGΔihfA strain, generated small colonies upon overnight incubation.
source: Corroborating with this finding, we show that ΔspeGΔfis, but not ΔspeGΔihfA strain, generated small colonies upon overnight incubation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the role of Fis regulator is critical under spermidine stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The role of Fis regulator is critical under spermidine stress.
source: Corroborating with this finding, we show that ΔspeGΔfis, but not ΔspeGΔihfA strain, generated small colonies upon overnight incubation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the role of Fis regulator is critical under spermidine stress.
evidence: This is an inference from the growth data of the mutant strains.

claim: None of the three critical genes (soxS, sodA, and zwf) was found to be activated in the microarray.
source: Surprisingly, none of the three critical genes was found to be activated in the microarray.
evidence: This is an observation from the microarray data.

claim: RT-qPCR analyses verified the unaltered expression of soxS, sodA, and zwf under spermidine stress.
source: RT-qPCR analyses verified the unaltered expression of soxS, sodA, and zwf under spermidine stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No transcriptional activation of soxS and sodA promoters was found under spermidine stress.
source: Consistently, using ΔspeG harboring pUA66_soxS, a reporter plasmid expressing gfpmut2 from the soxS promoter (PsoxS-gfpmut2), and RKM1 strain containing a chromosomally fused lacZ reporter under sodA promoter (PsodA-lacZ) (Table 1), we did not find any transcriptional activation of soxS and sodA promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spermidine in excess blocks the O2--mediated activation of SoxR.
source: Therefore, we suspected whether spermidine in excess blocks the O2- -mediated activation of SoxR, thereby aggravating O2- toxicity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observed data.

claim: Spermidine suppressed the menadione-induced GFP reporter fluorescence.
source: Spermidine also suppressed the menadione-induced GFP reporter fluorescence (Figure 4B), suggesting that spermidine indeed blocks SoxR-mediated activation of soxS in E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Spermidine blocks SoxR-mediated activation of soxS in E. coli.
source: Spermidine also suppressed the menadione-induced GFP reporter fluorescence (Figure 4B), suggesting that spermidine indeed blocks SoxR-mediated activation of soxS in E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference from the reporter assay data.

claim: The catalase coding genes (katE and katG) were downregulated under spermidine stress.
source: Among other ROS-responsive genes, the catalase coding genes (katE and katG) were downregulated (Figure 4A), while no change was observed in the expression of ahpCF genes under spermidine stress (GEO accession #154618).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No change was observed in the expression of ahpCF genes under spermidine stress.
source: Among other ROS-responsive genes, the catalase coding genes (katE and katG) were downregulated (Figure 4A), while no change was observed in the expression of ahpCF genes under spermidine stress (GEO accession #154618).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data.

claim: Western blotting experiments exhibited the unchanged expression of SodA in the spermidine-treated ΔspeG strain compared to untreated counterparts.
source: Consistent with the microarray expressions, our western blotting experiments exhibited the unchanged expression of SodA and a decreased expression of KatG in the spermidine-treated ΔspeG strain compared to untreated counterparts (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Western blotting experiments exhibited a decreased expression of KatG in the spermidine-treated ΔspeG strain compared to untreated counterparts.
source: Consistent with the microarray expressions, our western blotting experiments exhibited the unchanged expression of SodA and a decreased expression of KatG in the spermidine-treated ΔspeG strain compared to untreated counterparts (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 4D.
